title: TeamTNT_Hildegard_Incident_Response_Scenario_562
description: Investigate and respond to a TeamTNT Hildegard backdoor compromise using standard incident response procedures.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content:
The target network has been compromised by the TeamTNT malware family, specifically the Hildegard backdoor. This malware is known to establish command and control (C2) connections through tmate reverse shells and Internet Relay Chat (IRC) channels. It disguises itself using legitimate Linux process names and employs library injection techniques.

Your task is to investigate and respond to this incident, following standard incident response procedures to contain and eradicate the threat. Submit the name of the suspicious service as a text value.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content:
You have SSH access to the target host with the following credentials:
- Hostname: target
- Username: cyrano
- Password: cyrano

From this host, you can SSH to other hosts in the network using the same credentials.

Enter the passkey 'start' as a text value to begin the scenario.
levels.local_content:
Local sandbox access is not required for this scenario. Use the following credentials to access the target host:
- Username: cyrano
- Password: cyrano

Enter the passkey 'start' as a text value to begin the scenario.

levels.title: Investigate Suspicious Services
levels.content:
Investigate the target host for suspicious services or processes.

Objective: Identify any unauthorized or suspicious services running on the target host.

Hint: Check running services and processes, looking for anything unusual or unexpected.

Submit the name of the suspicious service as a text value.
levels.solution: To investigate suspicious services, you can use commands like `ps aux`, `top`, or `systemctl list-units --type=service`. Look for any services or processes that seem unusual or unexpected, such as those using high CPU or memory resources, or those with unfamiliar names or paths.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Start by examining the running services and processes on the system.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Look for any services or processes that seem unusual or unexpected, such as those using high CPU or memory resources, or those with unfamiliar names or paths.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: The suspicious service might be disguised as a legitimate system service. Pay close attention to services with unusual paths or those that do not match known system services.

levels.title: Determine Persistence Mechanism
levels.content:
Determine how the suspicious service is automatically started after reboot.

Objective: Identify the persistence mechanism used by the suspicious service.

Hint: Investigate systemd services, cron jobs, or other scheduled tasks.

Submit the name of the persistence mechanism service as a text value.
levels.solution: To determine the persistence mechanism, you can investigate systemd services, cron jobs, or other scheduled tasks. Use commands like `systemctl list-unit-files --type=service`, `crontab -l`, or `ls /etc/cron.*` to look for any entries related to the suspicious service.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Begin by examining systemd services, cron jobs, or other scheduled tasks.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Look for any entries related to the suspicious service in systemd services, cron jobs, or other scheduled tasks.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: The persistence mechanism might involve a systemd service that starts automatically. Check the status and dependencies of the suspicious service.

levels.title: Locate Malicious Artifacts
levels.content:
Locate the executable or file associated with the suspicious activity.

Objective: Correlate processes with files on disk and identify malicious artifacts.

Hint: Search for files related to the suspicious service or process.

Submit the path to the malicious artifact as a text value.
levels.solution: To locate malicious artifacts, you can search for files related to the suspicious service or process. Use commands like `find / -name "*tmux*" 2>/dev/null`, `locate tmux`, or `grep -r "tmux" /etc/` to search for relevant files.

hints.title: First hint title
hints.content: Start by searching for files related to the suspicious service or process.

hints.title: Second hint title
hints.content: Look for files with unusual names, paths, or contents that may be related to the suspicious service or process.

hints.title: Third hint title
hints.content: The malicious artifact might be a script or binary located in an unusual directory. Pay close attention to files with names that do not match typical system files.
